This vignette follows one HTAN dataset from a metadata query to a
biological result. It picks a small open spatial transcriptomics dataset,
confirms where it came from, downloads it, reads it into a
`SpatialExperiment`, wraps it with clinical data in a
`MultiAssayExperiment`, and runs a short analysis: quality control,
normalisation, clustering and spatial plots. Along the way it explains why
each step is done the way it is.

It assumes the [introduction](HTAN.html) and the
[data model vignette](data-model.html). The download step needs a free
Synapse account and a personal access token in `SYNAPSE_AUTH_TOKEN` (see
the introduction).


``` r
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(scuttle)
library(scran)
library(scater)
library(bluster)
library(HTAN)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
con <- htan_con("r7")
```

The order matters: the Bioconductor packages attach functions named
`count()`, `desc()`, `slice()` and `rename()` that mask dplyr's, so dplyr
is attached last.

# Choosing a dataset

## The question

The Vanderbilt atlas (HTA11) studied colorectal precancer: adenomatous and
serrated polyps, the lesions from which most colorectal cancers arise. A
polyp is a good first spatial dataset. Its tissue has an obvious
architecture (epithelial crypts, the stroma of the lamina propria, immune
aggregates), so a correct analysis should recover recognisable regions, and
a premalignant lesion is exactly the kind of transition HTAN was set up to
study.

## Finding candidate files

10x Visium measures the transcriptome in a grid of 55 µm spots across a
tissue section. Level 4 Visium files are processed objects, ready to
analyse. Here are the open ones, smallest first:


``` r
visium <- htan_files(
    assay == "10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-RNA-seq", level == 4,
    access == "open-synapse", con = con)
visium |>
    count(HTAN_Center, extension) |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   HTAN_Center     extension     n
#>   <chr>           <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 HTAN WUSTL      .rds        132
#> 2 HTAN Vanderbilt .h5ad        43
visium |>
    filter(extension == ".h5ad", n_participants == 1) |>
    arrange(File_Size) |>
    select(HTAN_Data_File_ID, Filename, File_Size) |>
    head(5) |>
    collect()
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   HTAN_Data_File_ID            Filename                                File_Size
#>   <chr>                        <chr>                                       <dbl>
#> 1 HTA11_7862_200000101134111   visium_level_4/8270_AS_1_unfiltered.h5…  13075894
#> 2 HTA11_6134_200000101134111   visium_level_4/8270_AS_5_unfiltered.h5…  13437865
#> 3 HTA11_10711_200000101134111  visium_level_4/8270_AS_2_unfiltered.h5…  13753214
#> 4 HTA11_8622_200000102134111   visium_level_4/7319_AS_3_unfiltered.h5…  17443425
#> 5 HTA11_99999974143_8462034111 visium_level_4/7003_AS_1_unfiltered.h5…  19035870
```

Two things guide the choice. First, the format: `.h5ad` (AnnData) files
follow a common layout that anndataR reads reliably, whereas `.rds` files
hold whatever R object the center saved. Second, size and provenance: a
file from a single participant, and small enough to download in seconds.
The smallest single-participant `.h5ad` qualifies:


``` r
visium_id <- "HTA11_7862_200000101134111"
file <- htan_files(HTAN_Data_File_ID == visium_id, con = con) |> collect()
glimpse(select(file, HTAN_Data_File_ID, Filename, File_Size, md5,
    entityId, HTAN_Participant_ID, HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID, access))
#> Rows: 1
#> Columns: 8
#> $ HTAN_Data_File_ID           <chr> "HTA11_7862_200000101134111"
#> $ Filename                    <chr> "visium_level_4/8270_AS_1_unfiltered.h5ad"
#> $ File_Size                   <dbl> 13075894
#> $ md5                         <chr> "dadd45c1853c1bc56eb546182b02ea4f"
#> $ entityId                    <chr> "syn51133587"
#> $ HTAN_Participant_ID         <chr> "HTA11_7862"
#> $ HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID <chr> "HTA11_7862_2000001011"
#> $ access                      <chr> "open-synapse"
```

The `entityId` is its Synapse ID; `access` is `open-synapse`, so a token is
needed but no data access request.

## What the metadata say about it

The assay table holds the processing details:


``` r
htan_tbl("10xvisium_spatialtranscriptomics_scRNAseq_level4_metadata",
    con) |>
    filter(HTAN_Data_File_ID == visium_id) |>
    select(Workflow_Version, Visium_Workflow_Type,
        Visium_Workflow_Parameters_Description, Run_ID, Data_Release) |>
    collect() |>
    glimpse()
#> Rows: 1
#> Columns: 5
#> $ Workflow_Version                       <chr> "spaceranger-1.3.0"
#> $ Visium_Workflow_Type                   <chr> "Spaceranger 1.3.0"
#> $ Visium_Workflow_Parameters_Description <chr> "transcriptome -- GRCh38-2020-A…
#> $ Run_ID                                 <chr> "8270-AS"
#> $ Data_Release                           <chr> "Release 5.0"
```

Space Ranger 1.3.0 against GRCh38-2020-A, with the human whole-transcriptome
probe set, so this is the probe-based Visium chemistry. "Unfiltered" in the
file name
suggests it holds every spot on the capture area, not only those under
tissue, which the analysis will need to handle.

# Tracing lineage

Before using a processed file, check what it was made from:


``` r
lineage <- htan_lineage(visium_id, con = con) |>
    arrange(depth, related_file_id) |>
    collect()
lineage |>
    transmute(depth, Component = sub("10xVisiumSpatialTranscriptomics-",
        "", Component), file = basename(Filename))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   depth Component     file                                
#>   <int> <chr>         <chr>                               
#> 1    -3 RNA-seqLevel1 8270-AS-0001_S1_L005_R1_001.fastq.gz
#> 2    -3 RNA-seqLevel1 8270-AS-0001_S1_L005_R2_001.fastq.gz
#> 3    -2 RNA-seqLevel2 8270_AS_1_possorted_genome_bam.bam  
#> 4    -1 RNA-seqLevel3 8270_AS_1_barcodes.tsv.gz           
#> 5    -1 RNA-seqLevel3 8270_AS_1_features.tsv.gz           
#> 6    -1 RNA-seqLevel3 8270_AS_1_matrix.mtx.gz             
#> 7    -1 RNA-seqLevel3 8270_AS_1_tissue_positions_list.csv 
#> 8     0 RNA-seqLevel4 8270_AS_1_unfiltered.h5ad
```

FASTQ (Level 1, controlled), aligned BAM (Level 2, controlled), the Space
Ranger output (Level 3, open) and this object (Level 4). All were measured
on one biospecimen. Its record, and the participant's:


``` r
biospecimen <- htan_tbl("biospecimen", con) |>
    filter(HTAN_Biospecimen_ID == !!file$HTAN_Assayed_Biospecimen_ID) |>
    select(HTAN_Biospecimen_ID, HTAN_Parent_ID, Acquisition_Method_Type,
        Preservation_Method, Tumor_Tissue_Type, Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy,
        Histologic_Morphology_Code) |>
    collect()
glimpse(biospecimen)
#> Rows: 1
#> Columns: 7
#> $ HTAN_Biospecimen_ID         <chr> "HTA11_7862_2000001011"
#> $ HTAN_Parent_ID              <chr> "HTA11_7862"

htan_tbl("clinical_tier1_demographics", con) |>

    select(HTAN_Participant_ID, Gender, Race, Vital_Status) |>

#> # A tibble: 1 × 4

#>   <chr>               <chr>  <chr>                     <chr>       
#> 1 HTA11_7862          Male   black or african american Alive
```

The section is a fresh biopsy of a premalignant lesion of the sigmoid
colon, with morphology code `M82110`: ICD-O-3 8211/0, tubular adenoma. The
participant's diagnosis record is "Not Reported" throughout (see the
[data model vignette](data-model.html#a-visium-spatial-transcriptomics-object-back-to-the-patient)),
so the histology comes from the biospecimen. The participant has other
data too, which could extend this analysis later:


``` r
htan_files(participants = file$HTAN_Participant_ID, con = con) |>
    count(Component, access) |>
    arrange(Component) |>
    collect()
```

# Downloading

`htan_download()` checks the access tier and total size, asks Synapse for
a short-lived download URL, fetches the file, and verifies its md5 against
the metadata. A second call finds the verified copy and does not download
again.


``` r
dest <- file.path(tempdir(), "htan-data")
dl <- htan_download(file, dest = dest, con = con)
dl
```

# Reading into a SpatialExperiment

`read_htan()` reads `.h5ad` files with anndataR. When the AnnData object
has a `spatial` embedding (the layout scanpy writes for Visium), the result
is a `SpatialExperiment` with the spot positions as `spatialCoords()`:


``` r
spe <- read_htan(dl)
spe
```

Level 4 objects differ between centers, so look before you compute. Three
things matter here: which assay holds raw counts, whether there are spot
coordinates, and which spots are under tissue.


``` r
assayNames(spe)
names(colData(spe))
names(rowData(spe))
head(rownames(spe))
is(spe, "SpatialExperiment")
```

Marker genes are easier to read as symbols. If the row names are Ensembl
IDs, use a symbol column from `rowData()` instead (scanpy and Space Ranger
call it different things), keeping names unique:


``` r
if (mean(grepl("^ENSG", rownames(spe))) > 0.5) {
    symbol_col <- intersect(c("gene_symbols", "gene_name", "feature_name",
        "symbol", "gene_ids"), names(rowData(spe)))[1]
    rownames(spe) <- make.unique(as.character(rowData(spe)[[symbol_col]]))
}
head(rownames(spe))
```

anndataR maps AnnData's main matrix `X` to an assay named `X`. Whether `X`
is raw counts or normalised values is the center's choice, so test it: raw
counts are whole numbers.


``` r
x <- assay(spe, "X")
sample_values <- as.numeric(x[, seq_len(min(200, ncol(x)))])
all(sample_values == round(sample_values))
assay(spe, "counts") <- x
assay(spe, "X") <- NULL
```

If this were `FALSE`, the counts would have to come from a layer of the
AnnData object or from the Level 3 Space Ranger matrix listed in the
lineage.

If the object had no spatial embedding, the spot positions are in the
Level 3 `tissue_positions_list.csv` from the lineage table, which can be
downloaded and joined by barcode. This chunk does that only when needed:


``` r
if (!is(spe, "SpatialExperiment")) {
    pos_id <- lineage$related_file_id[
        grepl("tissue_positions", lineage$Filename)]
    pos_dl <- htan_download(pos_id, dest = dest, con = con)
    pos <- read.csv(pos_dl$path, header = FALSE, col.names = c("barcode",
        "in_tissue", "array_row", "array_col", "pxl_row", "pxl_col"))
    pos <- pos[match(colnames(spe), pos$barcode), ]
    colData(spe)$in_tissue <- pos$in_tissue
    spe <- as(spe, "SpatialExperiment")
    spatialCoords(spe) <- as.matrix(pos[, c("pxl_col", "pxl_row")])
}
dim(spatialCoords(spe))
```

Finally, keep only spots under tissue. Spots outside the tissue capture
ambient RNA and would form their own spurious cluster:


``` r
if ("in_tissue" %in% names(colData(spe))) {
    print(table(in_tissue = spe$in_tissue))
    spe <- spe[, spe$in_tissue == 1]
}
dim(spe)
```

# Adding clinical context: a MultiAssayExperiment

`htan_experiment()` builds a `MultiAssayExperiment` from objects named by
their `HTAN_Data_File_ID`. It looks up each file's participant in
`id_provenance`, maps every spot to that participant in the `sampleMap`,
and fills `colData` with the participant's demographics and diagnosis.
Biospecimen annotation is per sample rather than per participant, so it is
added to the spots' own `colData` first:


``` r
for (field in c("HTAN_Biospecimen_ID", "Tumor_Tissue_Type",
    "Site_of_Resection_or_Biopsy", "Histologic_Morphology_Code")) {
    colData(spe)[[field]] <- biospecimen[[field]]
}
mae <- htan_experiment(setNames(list(spe), visium_id), con = con)
mae
MultiAssayExperiment::colData(mae)[, c("Gender", "Race", "Vital_Status",
    "Primary_Diagnosis")]
head(MultiAssayExperiment::sampleMap(mae))
```

With one file the container is small, but the structure is the point:
adding the participant's single-cell data, or other participants' Visium
sections, keeps every spot and cell linked to one clinical record. For a
file pooled from several participants, `htan_experiment()` needs the
`colData` column that names each cell's participant
(`participant_col`); see the [data model vignette](data-model.html#a-file-from-several-participants).

The analysis below works on the `SpatialExperiment` itself:


``` r
spe <- MultiAssayExperiment::experiments(mae)[[1]]
```

# Analysis

The steps follow the standard Bioconductor workflow for spot-based
spatial transcriptomics, as in the book *Orchestrating Spatial Transcriptomics
Analysis with Bioconductor* ([OSTA](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSTA/))
and its single-cell counterpart
([OSCA](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA/)), with choices
explained as they come.

## Quality control

Per-spot metrics: total counts (library size), the number of genes
detected, and the share of counts from mitochondrial genes, which rises in
damaged tissue.


``` r
is_mito <- grepl("^MT-", rownames(spe), ignore.case = TRUE)
sum(is_mito)
spe <- addPerCellQCMetrics(spe, subsets = list(mito = is_mito))
summary(spe$sum)
summary(spe$detected)
summary(spe$subsets_mito_percent)
```

Plotting the metrics on the tissue (image row coordinates increase
downwards, hence the reversed y axis) shows whether low-quality spots are
scattered (technical) or form a region (biological):


``` r
spot_coords <- function(spe) {
    xy <- as.data.frame(spatialCoords(spe))
    names(xy) <- c("x", "y")
    xy
}
spot_plot <- function(spe, values, name) {
    ggplot(cbind(spot_coords(spe), value = values),
        aes(x, y, colour = value)) +
        geom_point(size = 1) +
        scale_y_reverse() +
        coord_fixed() +
        labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = name) +
        theme_void()
}
spot_plot(spe, log10(spe$sum + 1), "log10\ncounts") +
    scale_colour_viridis_c()
```

Spots are flagged as outliers by median absolute deviations (MADs) from
the median, instead of fixed thresholds, because sensible thresholds depend
on the tissue, the probe panel and sequencing depth. Library size and
detected genes are tested on the low side only; mitochondrial share on the
high side.


``` r
discard <- perCellQCFilters(spe, sub.fields = "subsets_mito_percent")
colSums(as.matrix(discard))
spe <- spe[, !discard$discard]
dim(spe)
```

A polyp biopsy is small and mostly epithelium, so few spots should fail. A
large discarded fraction, or discarded spots forming a region, would call
for a closer look before dropping them.

## Normalisation

Spots differ in library size for technical reasons (capture efficiency,
tissue thickness) and biological ones (cell density). Library-size
normalisation followed by a log transform is the usual choice for Visium.
The pooling-based size factors common in single-cell work assume most
genes are not differentially expressed between pools of cells, which is
less safe for spots that mix several cells of different types.


``` r
spe <- computeLibraryFactors(spe)
spe <- logNormCounts(spe)
```

## Feature selection and dimensionality reduction

Highly variable genes carry the structure; the rest add noise. The variance
of each gene's log-expression is modelled against its mean, and the 2,000
genes with the largest biological component are kept. Mitochondrial genes
are excluded so that tissue damage does not drive the clustering.


``` r
dec <- modelGeneVar(spe[!is_mito, ])
hvgs <- getTopHVGs(dec, n = 2000)
head(hvgs, 20)
```


``` r
set.seed(1)
spe <- runPCA(spe, subset_row = hvgs, ncomponents = 30)
percent_var <- attr(reducedDim(spe, "PCA"), "percentVar")
round(head(percent_var, 10), 1)
```

The first components explain most of the variance; 30 are kept, a common
default that is generous for a tissue with a handful of domains.

## Clustering

Spots are clustered on the principal components with a shared
nearest-neighbour graph and the Louvain algorithm, as for single cells.
This uses expression alone; the spatial plot afterwards is then a test:
if clusters computed without coordinates form coherent regions, they
reflect real tissue structure. Spatially aware methods (for example
BayesSpace or Banksy) smooth over neighbours and would give cleaner
domains, at the cost of that independent check.


``` r
set.seed(1)
spe$cluster <- clusterCells(spe, use.dimred = "PCA",
    BLUSPARAM = NNGraphParam(k = 20, cluster.fun = "louvain"))
table(spe$cluster)
```


``` r
spot_plot(spe, spe$cluster, "Cluster") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3)))
```


``` r
set.seed(1)
spe <- runUMAP(spe, dimred = "PCA")
plotReducedDim(spe, "UMAP", colour_by = "cluster")
```

## What the clusters are

Marker genes for each cluster, from pairwise comparisons against the
others, say what each cluster is:


``` r
markers <- findMarkers(spe, groups = spe$cluster, test.type = "t",
    direction = "up", pval.type = "some")
top_markers <- vapply(markers, function(m) {
    paste(head(rownames(m), 8), collapse = ", ")
}, "")
tibble::tibble(cluster = names(top_markers), top_markers = top_markers)
```

Known markers of the colonic mucosa make the interpretation concrete:
`EPCAM` and `CEACAM5` for epithelium, `MUC2` for goblet cells, `LGR5` and
`OLFM4` for crypt-base stem cells (expanded in adenomas), `COL1A1` and
`VIM` for stroma, and `PTPRC` for immune cells.


``` r
genes <- intersect(c("EPCAM", "MUC2", "OLFM4", "LGR5", "COL1A1", "PTPRC"),
    rownames(spe))
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(genes, function(g) {
    cbind(spot_coords(spe), gene = g, logcounts = logcounts(spe)[g, ])
}))
ggplot(long, aes(x, y, colour = logcounts)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6) +
    scale_colour_viridis_c() +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    coord_fixed() +
    facet_wrap(~ gene) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_void()
```


``` r
plotDots(spe, features = genes, group = "cluster")
```



Read the plots together: a cluster high in `EPCAM` and `CEACAM5` (here
cluster <pending>) is epithelium; within the
epithelium, `OLFM4` and `LGR5` mark the proliferative, stem-like compartment
that expands in adenomas, and `MUC2` the differentiated goblet cells. Stroma
(`COL1A1`, `VIM`) and immune cells (`PTPRC`) lie between and beneath the
crypts. Whether the adenomatous epithelium separates from normal-looking
epithelium in this section is the kind of question to pursue next, with
the H&E image (an auxiliary file in the lineage) for reference.

# Where to go from here

- **More sections.** Other Vanderbilt Visium files cover more polyps
  (`visium` above). Read several, give each its file ID, and combine them
  in one `MultiAssayExperiment`; integrate them with batch correction
  (for example `batchelor::fastMNN`) before joint clustering.
- **Single-cell reference.** The participant also has single-cell
  RNA-seq (Level 3 count matrices for the polyp and for normal colon, and
  Vanderbilt's merged Level 4 objects). Cell types from those can be used
  to deconvolve the spots (for example with
  [SPOTlight](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/SPOTlight.html)).
- **Spatial domains and statistics.**
  [BayesSpace](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/BayesSpace.html)
  or [Banksy](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/Banksy.html)
  for spatially smoothed domains;
  [nnSVG](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/nnSVG.html)
  for spatially variable genes.
- **Other participants.** `htan_files()` and the clinical tables find
  comparable sections from other atlases, for example premalignant versus
  invasive tissue.

# Notes on reproducibility

The metadata release is pinned (`htan_con("r7")`), the file is identified
by its HTAN ID and checked against its md5, and random steps are seeded.
The software versions are below. What is not pinned is the file's content
on Synapse: if the center replaced it, the md5 check would fail rather than
silently give a different result.
